summary: I strongly support a 2030 ban because of the climate urgency, the local health benefits of less pollution near schools, and the practical financial case that EVs and renewables can lower household bills. I'm reassured by the focus on fairness — public ownership, insulation, public transport, grants and taxing the super‑rich — but I worry about implementation challenges like charging infrastructure, protecting jobs, and political and administrative deliverability, which could affect my support for the timing and details.

This message strengthens my support for a 2030 ban by framing the switch as urgently needed for the climate and immediately beneficial to public health and household budgets. I also appreciate that it pairs the ban with concrete protections (charging infrastructure, cheaper public transport for young and low-income people, and home insulation) and funding ideas (taxing the super-rich, public ownership of energy) that fit my fairness values, though I still want assurances jobs are protected and implementation is practical and equitable.

Reading that message reinforces why I feel this is urgent — as a parent who cares about the environment I want to protect children’s futures, cut household fuel costs, and improve air quality around schools, and I support funding the transition through wealth taxes rather than fossil‑fuel subsidies for reasons of social justice. I also stress fairness and remain wary about practical details — I want big public investment in insulation, affordable public transport, and adequate grants so a ban doesn’t hurt lower‑income families, and I’m concerned about how quickly rural transport and charging infrastructure and sufficient, possibly means‑tested, grants will be rolled out.

I support a ban by 2030 because, as a parent, I worry about my children’s air and climate and welcome cleaner streets, lower running costs, and concrete investments like charging points, better public transport, and home insulation that would make the transition fairer for low‑income families like mine in the South West. I’m still concerned about practical implementation — how quickly rural charging and public transport improvements will arrive and whether insulation and grant schemes will be means‑tested and generous enough so low‑income households aren’t left worse off — and those details will determine if I can fully back the ban.

I support the goals of protecting young people’s futures, cutting fuel costs, and improving air quality, but I worry a fast 2030 ban would unfairly price out moderate‑income households like mine unless grants, insulation, reliable public transport, and support for tradespeople and rural areas are truly in place. I find calls for a wealth tax and ending fossil‑fuel subsidies fair in principle, yet I’m skeptical about how realistically and efficiently such funding and public‑ownership plans would be implemented, so I’m open to the goal but uneasy about the speed and safeguards.

I feel more worried and conflicted about a 2030 ban: I support the goals of reducing pollution and protecting future generations, but I fear the timeline is too aggressive for modest‑income households, tradespeople, rural drivers and small businesses who may lack home charging or insulation. I want sensible, step‑by‑step change with strong safeguards—targeted grants, insulation, expanded charging and energy supply, and reliable funding—before I could back a tight ban.

I support tackling climate change and cleaner local air because it matters to me as a parent and nature-lover, and I appreciate linking a ban to practical benefits and fairness measures (grants, public transport, insulation, wealth taxes, ending fossil-fuel subsidies, public ownership, job guarantees) — but I remain worried about how quickly markets and infrastructure can adapt, especially for rural and poorly served areas. I’m also sharpened in my concern about fairness and practicality: a hard 2030 cutoff feels risky without funded plans for charging, second‑hand markets, protections for tradespeople and small businesses, and clear implementation details rather than dismissing climate goals as mere ideology.

Reading that message heightens my worries about fairness and practicality — I worry a 2030 ban could hit working families, rural residents, and tradespeople hard unless guarantees like grants, rural charging, robust second‑hand EV markets, exemptions or phased support, and cheaper public transport are in place. At the same time it nudges me toward conditional support because it links the ban to concrete benefits I care about (cleaner air, lower running costs) and sensible fairness measures, but I remain unconvinced without clear, well‑funded implementation that protects low‑income households, small businesses, and rural communities.

I support cleaner air and the long-term savings from EVs and public investment in insulation and transport, and I think ending fossil-fuel subsidies and taxing the very wealthy to fund the transition is reasonable if it truly protects modest-income households. But I worry a hard 2030 cutoff would unfairly hit ordinary families, tradespeople and rural areas that lack reliable charging or public transport, so I want phased measures, better grants, second‑hand support and stronger local infrastructure before any strict ban.

I support the goal of cleaner air and lower emissions, but reading this has made me more worried that a blunt 2030 ban would be unfair and too soon for rural areas, tradespeople, and ordinary families who can’t afford new EVs without much better local charging, support for the second‑hand market, and generous targeted grants. I want a phased approach with real investment and safeguards—funded fairly, e.g. by taxing the wealthy—so the transition protects people like me in the East of England rather than leaving them worse off.

I accept the environmental case and lower running costs, since I worry about bills and my neighbourhood’s health, but a 2030 ban feels rushed and risks forcing people like me on modest incomes into unaffordable choices unless there are clear, practical supports. I want major public investment—grants, better public transport, home insulation and charging infrastructure—and evidence that any new taxes or ending of subsidies will be spent effectively to protect ordinary families, otherwise rural and suburban areas in the East Midlands will be left behind.

I appreciate the environmental and health benefits and the idea of fair investment to help people switch, but a 2030 ban feels abrupt for me given my income and location in the East Midlands. I’m concerned about upfront costs, local charging reliability, and whether grants or improved public transport will arrive in time, so I’d support the policy only if the timetable and targeted support are realistic and evidence-based.

I’m sympathetic to the goal of cleaner air near schools, lower running costs from electric cars, and protecting young people’s futures, but I want assurances that fairness and a just transition are central so ordinary families aren’t unfairly burdened. I prefer funding through taxing the very wealthy and ending fossil-fuel subsidies, but I need clear details on timelines, grants, and support for rural and lower-income households before I’d fully back a 2030 deadline.

I’m sympathetic to the goal — cleaner air near schools, lower running costs with electric cars, and protecting kids’ futures all appeal to me — but I worry a hard 2030 ban is risky unless there are clear, funded measures to help ordinary families afford EVs, improve public transport, and insulate homes so costs aren’t simply shifted onto people like me. Taxing the very wealthy and reinvesting profits into communities sounds more acceptable than regressive measures, but I’d need clearer details on timelines, grants, and support for rural households before I’d feel comfortable with that deadline.

I still strongly want climate action and cleaner air for my grandchildren, and I’m persuaded that EVs and renewables can cut running costs and pollution. Knowing the plan stresses fairness — public ownership of transport, big insulation programs, reliable affordable buses, grants, and funding via wealth taxes — eases my worries about upfront costs and access, though I remain concerned it could harm working families without those protections.

I'm cautiously more positive about the ban because the health, pollution, and cost-saving arguments resonate with me and the proposed EVs, public transport, and chargers address bill concerns. I still worry about implementation — I need guarantees on chargers, affordable travel, home insulation, and funding via wealth tax/public ownership so the transition doesn't unfairly burden modest-income communities like mine.

I support the environmental goals—cleaner air, lower running costs, and tackling climate change—especially because proposals for fairness like investing in public transport, home insulation, and grants would help people like me on a low income avoid being priced out of switching to an EV or losing mobility. I also back funding the transition by taxing the super-rich and ending fossil fuel subsidies, but I’m cautious about the ambitious 2030 timeline unless charging infrastructure, affordable EVs, and targeted financial support are in place quickly enough to prevent disruption.

I support the focus on cleaner air near schools and hospitals and the cost savings, and I appreciate that the ban is paired with practical supports like charging infrastructure, cheap public transport for young and low-income people, and home insulation because a strict 2030 ban could be unfair if alternatives aren’t affordable. Funding through wealth taxes and publicly owned energy seems fair, but I need clearer, faster implementation details to be confident the timeline won’t leave low-income people stranded.

Reading that message reinforces my worries that a 2030 ban would feel like a Westminster-imposed policy that misunderstands rural life, small businesses, and low-income people who need affordable, reliable vehicles and may not afford electric alternatives. I care about the environment, but I’d find the policy more acceptable only with strong financial support, investment in domestic energy and charging infrastructure, and exemptions or longer lead times for those who genuinely rely on petrol vehicles.

Reading this makes me more uneasy about a 2030 ban because it feels like a Westminster order that overlooks rural life and small businesses — it highlights plumbers, delivery drivers and families who can’t easily charge at home and worries me that many on modest incomes couldn’t afford expensive upgrades without major help. I care about the environment but I’d prefer measures that protect jobs, give longer lead times, provide strong financial support for low‑income households and tradespeople, and invest in rural charging and domestic energy instead of an immediate blanket ban.

I support the climate and public-health goals—cleaner air near schools, lower household running costs, and the stated fairness and support for people facing upfront costs—but I remain concerned the 2030 deadline is too tight for many families like mine, especially in rural Wales with limited charging and modest incomes. I’d back the plan only with clear, funded roll-out of chargers, targeted grants for lower- and middle-income households, stronger public transport and home-insulation programs, and guarantees that shifting subsidies and taxing the wealthy won’t unduly burden pensioners, rural households, or those who can’t easily switch vehicles.

I support the ambition for cleaner air near schools, lower household running costs, and complementary investments (chargers, public transport, insulation) as fair and aligned with my values, and I like funding via a wealth tax and public ownership. However, I’m uneasy about the 2030 deadline for rural Wales—I'd need funded plans for rapid rural charger rollout, targeted grants for lower-/middle-income households (including pensioners), and stronger insulation and bus-service measures before fully backing that timeline.

I support phasing out new petrol cars by 2030 because it aligns with my commitment to protecting the environment and improving air quality, and I’m persuaded by the jobs and household‑bill savings it could bring. However, I’m concerned about fairness and implementation—without public investment in insulation, grants, reliable public transport and rapid roll‑out of affordable EVs and charging, a fast ban could unfairly burden ordinary families, rural residents and small businesses.

I’m sympathetic to the environmental case for phasing out new petrol cars by 2030 and agree it could improve air quality, cut household fuel bills and create clean‑jobs. But I’m worried a hard ban would unfairly burden working families, tradespeople and rural drivers unless cheap EVs, a strong second‑hand market, rapid rural charging and well‑funded protections (grants, insulation, public transport, support for small businesses) are guaranteed — so I’d only back a firm target conditional on those measures and fair funding.

Reading this makes me more persuaded that a 2030 ban could deliver tangible benefits for families—lower running costs, cleaner air near schools, and clearer climate action—which fits my view that government should shape better conditions. I insist the policy include strong public investment (insulation, public transport), protections for low-income households, and funding focused on the wealthy, with public ownership and just-transition measures to prevent people being priced out or left without viable transport options.

I’m increasingly convinced a 2030 ban is practical and socially beneficial, especially for lower running costs and cleaner air near schools. My support hinges on strong accompanying investments (chargers, affordable public transport, home insulation) funded by a wealth tax and public ownership so the transition doesn’t harm low-income families.

I support the ambition because the climate and air-quality gains and lower running costs match my concern for protecting the planet and helping ordinary people, and I like the funding idea of asking the super-rich to help pay for the transition as it fits my redistributive, left-leaning views. My main caveat is that fairness and support matter: without strong public investment in insulation, reliable affordable public transport, grants for lower-income households, and scalable infrastructure and supply chains, a fast ban could feel punitive and risk creating new inequalities for renters and people who can’t easily change cars.

This pushes me toward supporting a 2030 ban because it links environmental gains to concrete social benefits I care about — less air pollution near schools and hospitals, lower running costs, and protections for lower‑income people. I’m reassured by the repeated call for investment in charging, affordable public transport, and home insulation, but I still worry about rollout practicality (infrastructure, supply chains, renters and those who can’t easily change vehicles), so my support depends on strong, well‑funded complementary measures.

I see the environmental and health benefits—lower running costs for EVs, cleaner air near schools, and tackling climate risks—and I appreciate the fairness arguments for public ownership, big insulation and transport investment, and taxing the super-rich to fund a just transition. But I’m worried about the practical cost for my household, the timeline, and whether grants and reliable, affordable public transport where I live will be enough, so I need clearer guarantees that low-income families won’t be left paying the bill.

Hearing this makes me more torn: I want a fairer, greener future for my family — cheaper running costs for EVs, cleaner air around schools, and health protections appeal to me, and I welcome investment in charging points, public transport, and home insulation funded by taxing the very wealthy. But I remain worried about practicalities for someone on our income — I need clear, enforceable guarantees of affordable support for low‑income households, a realistic infrastructure rollout in the North West, and strong protections so costs don’t just shift onto families like mine.

I support a 2030 ban because it would cut household fuel bills, clean the air around schools, and help address broader cost pressures like rents and food by reducing fossil‑fuel exposure. I value the focus on a just transition — public ownership, insulation, affordable public transport, targeted subsidies funded by wealthier households — though I want careful scrutiny of the funding and speed of infrastructure roll‑out so rural and low‑income families aren’t unfairly burdened.

I like that a 2030 ban gives a clear deadline and promises lower household running costs, cleaner air near schools and hospitals, and broader public‑health gains, which makes the policy feel practical and fair. The “just transition” measures and funding via taxing the wealthy align with my left‑leaning values and ease my main worries about rural and low‑income families—provided credible plans and timelines for charging, grid upgrades, rural transport, insulation, and targeted subsidies are delivered.

I support an early ban in principle because it would cut running costs with EVs, clean air around schools, and reduce climate-driven economic harms, which aligns with my general desire to protect the natural world even if it’s not my main focus. I care strongly about fairness and practical support—public ownership of key transport services, major insulation investment, better affordable public transport, grants, ending fossil-fuel subsidies, and funding a just transition (e.g., via a wealth tax) would reassure me, though I’d need clear implementation plans showing costs won’t unduly burden families like mine.

I’m more positive about a 2030 ban because of the climate and health benefits (cleaner air near schools, lower EV running costs) and the practical framing rather than it being merely symbolic. My main concern is affordability and fairness — I’d support it only if there are concrete plans for charging infrastructure, better public transport, home insulation and direct support funded so costs don’t fall disproportionately on ordinary households; proposals like a wealth tax and public ownership appeal to my slightly left-of-centre instincts but need detailed guarantees.

I support the green, community-focused goals—protecting young people’s futures, cutting bills, and improving air quality—but I need fairness and a just transition to ensure lower‑income families like mine aren’t left without affordable transport. Proposals for public ownership, big investment in insulation and public transport, grants, and taxing the super‑rich make me cautiously open to the policy, provided practical details (affordability of EVs, rural transport reliability, and timely delivery of measures) are clearly guaranteed and enforceable.

I support the intent because it aligns with my concern for the environment, cleaner air around schools and hospitals, and making life fairer by lowering running costs, but I’m wary about practicalities like how quickly affordable EVs will reach modest-income households and whether rural areas will get reliable alternatives to car dependence. The emphasis on real investment, protections for low‑income families—free or very cheap public transport, massive home insulation, guaranteed charging—and funding through taxing the wealthy and public ownership of energy makes the plan feel more just, though I’d need strong, enforceable guarantees that promised funding arrives and no one is left behind.

I strongly support a 2030 ban because it delivers concrete benefits I care about—lower household fuel bills, cleaner air around schools, and a climate-safe future—while emphasizing fairness through public ownership of transport, major insulation programmes, affordable reliable transit, and grants so low-income households aren’t left behind. I also back ending fossil subsidies and funding a just transition via wealth taxes, though I remain concerned about practical readiness of charging infrastructure and supply chains and whether the package will truly protect people who rely on older vehicles.

This strengthens my support for a 2030 ban because it ties the policy to outcomes I care about—lower household running costs, cleaner air near schools and hospitals, and urgent climate action—while pairing the ban with concrete fairness measures like charging infrastructure, free/cheap public transport for low‑income and young people, and large home‑insulation programmes so people aren’t left behind. I also welcome funding ideas (wealth taxes, public ownership of energy) that fit my left‑wing view that the rich and public systems should bear the burden, but I still worry whether charging networks and supply chains can scale by 2030 and whether support will arrive fast and sufficient enough to prevent hardship for those who depend on older cars.

This message reinforces my belief that phasing out petrol cars is crucial for tackling the climate emergency and improving local air quality, and I strongly value the environmental and public-health case. I also welcome the focus on fairness — grants, public ownership, insulation investment, better public transit, and funding via a wealth tax align with my left-leaning priorities — while remaining cautious about ambitious timelines like 2030 given concerns about infrastructure, affordability, and support for vulnerable people.

I believe banning new petrol car sales by 2030 is the urgent, practical climate action we need because it would cut pollution near schools and hospitals and save money through cheaper EVs and better public transport. But my support hinges on fairness and delivery — I worry a bare ban would punish low-income households, so I’m only more positive if it’s paired with well-funded charging, public-transport concessions, home insulation, and funding measures that ensure timely, equitable implementation.

I support the goals of protecting young people’s futures, cutting fuel costs, and reducing pollution, and I generally back moving away from fossil fuels because renewables and EVs are cheaper to run long-term. However, as someone with a low household income I'm worried about upfront EV costs and tight timelines, so I want grants, insulation investment, public ownership, affordable public transport, and wealth-tax-funded support to ensure a fair, properly funded transition by 2030.

I support cleaner air near schools and lower running costs from EVs because they align with my desire for a better future for my children. I’m concerned about upfront costs and whether promised support—grants, affordable public transport, home insulation, or wealth‑tax/public‑ownership funding—will actually reach low‑income people like me, and I need clearer guarantees on infrastructure and timelines so no one is left stranded by 2030.
